scripts/ci_local.sh --with-all --with-e2e reported all local CI gates passed.

So there is no defect to chase from the run, and Slice 50 starts from a clean baseline.

What the tree says is next
Stage 3 is closed as of Slice 49. The plan's own What is still open section and Slice 49's Carried list agree on what remains in the menu:

The kitchen's 86 panel does not group by heading — named as "the last surface that reads the menu flat" now that the guest menu is complete.
§16.3 has no scenario for either resequencing verb — "the largest end-to-end gap in the menu".
The wide layout stacks each row's three controls; the handheld barrier visits neither section surface.
Stage 4 (images) is the next stage, but it's a migration + route + CSP + upload question — a whole slice on its own.
The finding I found while reading, which decides the slice
TableOrderSurface.razor's GroupedMenu is a private property inside a Razor component, and it implements §11.1's grouping plus §7's two opposite-pointing rules (an inactive item stays and is marked; an inactive heading vanishes entirely) — the pair the specification restates every time it mentions them because both are easy to lose.

The tree states the rule against exactly this three times: §16.1 records there is no bUnit; KitchenQueue's own summary says "a rule that can only be checked by rendering a Razor component is a rule nobody checks" and names OrderStaging and OrderNarrative as the other two pure functions; and F-59 exists because a property everything assumed and nothing stated is a property nothing can catch. That walk has been asserted by nothing but scenario 17 — a browser and a database and two and a half minutes — since Slice 40.

And the kitchen needs the same walk with the opposite rule about hidden headings. A private property cannot be called from a second component, so grouping the 86 panel without repairing this means pasting the walk — which is F-59's mechanism precisely.

There's a smaller second half: the walk's doc comment claims it takes each heading's name and description "from the first row of each run". It assigns on every row, so it takes them from the last. Harmless only because the INNER JOIN guarantees the rows of a run agree — which is exactly why no test could ever have failed on it.

That's F-100, and it makes the 86 panel the right menu progress rather than an arbitrary pick.

The shape I'm going to build
New src/MyRestaurant.WebApplication/Menu/MenuGrouping.cs — the walk as a pure function, the fourth member of the OrderStaging / OrderNarrative / KitchenQueue set, with MenuHeadingGroup replacing the component-private MenuSectionOnTheMenu. Two named entry points — VisibleToGuests and EveryHeading — rather than a boolean, because a boolean at a call site is a rule nobody can read.
TableOrderSurface.razor calls it; behaviour identical.
KitchenBoard.razor's 86 panel groups by heading, showing headings hidden from guests marked rather than dropped — because 86ing is the kitchen's statement about stock, §7 says switching a heading off does not cascade to its items, and this panel is the only surface that can see or change those flags.
New tests/MyRestaurant.WebApplication.Tests/Menu/MenuGroupingTests.cs — the rule finally reachable without a browser.
TestingSectionContractTests' MinimumCountedClasses 24 → 25.
Full documentation: spec v1.35 (§11.2, §16.4, Appendix A F-100, changelog), DOCUMENTATION_REVIEW.md, BUILD_PROGRESS.md, MENU_AND_HANDHELD_PLAN.md, _CHANGES.md.
One decision I'll flag rather than make silently: ADR-0014's Context sentence "the kitchen's 86 panel is a flat <ul>" stays as written, because it records what was true when the decision was made — the same clause says the guest picker is a <select>, which stopped being true in Slice 39 and was correctly left alone.

Say the word and I'll author the archive — full files, repo-relative paths, extractable at the repository root in one operation, with the file accounting and the predicted test count stated. No bespoke text-manipulation scripts.
